claims.claim: Sort the cells in your body by size, from red blood cells up, and something odd turns up: each size class weighs roughly the same. (Hook, A4: what a viewer who swipes away at second two keeps.)
claims.note: A viewer who leaves here keeps: binned by size from red blood cells up, each size class of your cells weighs roughly the same. The paper's own headline says this without qualification: abstract 'all cells within a given logarithmic size class contribute an equal fraction to the body's total cellular biomass'; Results 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class (Fig. 4A)'; Conclusion 'cell biomass is roughly independent of cell-size class'. 'Roughly' is load-bearing: Fig. 4 shows class weights spread over about 0.2-7 kg in the male, and the paper says 'all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude' outside the gap. 'From red blood cells up' matches the binning ('only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells'). Female and child are 'broadly similar', so 'your body' is not limited to the reference man. 'Something odd' is the paper's 'surprising inverse relation'. Nothing false is left behind at second two.

claims.claim: A twenty twenty-three study
claims.note: PNAS 120(39) e2303077120, published online 18 Sep 2023 (issue 26 Sep 2023).

claims.claim: ...combined over fifteen hundred published sources
claims.note: Abstract: 'data drawn from >1,500 published sources'; Methods: 'more than 1,500 published sources'. 'Published sources' (not 'studies') matches; they include ICRP reference catalogues.

claims.claim: 1,500+ SOURCES
claims.note: As claim 3: '>1,500 published sources'.

claims.claim: ...to estimate the body's cells, type by type, and sorted them by size.
claims.note: 'we estimate total body counts'; cell size and count for ~400 cell types / 1,264 cell groups; Fig. 3 bins them into 26 logarithmic size classes. 'Estimate' matches the paper's own verb.

claims.claim: The smallest cells it sorted are red blood cells.
claims.note: 'Our size distribution does not include these small cells [platelets, haploid sperm, near 1e-11 g], and only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells (4 x 10^-11 g)'; Methods: 'We ignored binning cells smaller than erythrocytes'. 'It sorted' correctly limits this to the binned cells; Fig. 3's first bin starts at the red-cell lower bound.

claims.claim: RED BLOOD CELLS
claims.note: As claim 6.

claims.claim: The biggest are muscle fibres, more than a million times heavier.
claims.note: 'from a tiny red blood cell to a myocyte, more than a million-fold larger'; sizes run 'from red blood cells to the largest muscle fibers' over 'seven orders of magnitude'. The paper's size measure is mass in grams, so 'heavier' is the same claim. Fig. 3: myocytes (orange) occupy the top size classes up to ~2.7e-3 g.
Paper: 'more than a million-fold larger'; 4e-11 g to ~1e-4 g (myocyte peak) is 2.5e6, and the largest fibres reach ~1e-3 g. A floor, correctly marked '>'.

claims.claim: Now put those cells into size classes, where each class holds cells twice as heavy as the one before.
claims.note: Methods: 'bins increase by a multiplicative factor of 2 from small to large (octave size classes), beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'. SI: 'each larger size class twice as large as the adjacent smaller size class'.

claims.claim: ×2 CELL SIZE
claims.note: As claim 10; 'size' is cell mass, the paper's size measure.

claims.claim: Each time the size doubles, there are, on average, about half as many cells.
claims.note: Fig. 3: count per class vs cell mass, 'slope near -0.97' (95% CI -1.09 to -0.87). 2^-0.97 = 0.51 per doubling (0.47-0.55 across the CI), so 'about half'. 'On average' is right: Fig. 3 bins scatter around the fit (e.g. ~10x below near 1e-5 g).

claims.claim: HALF AS MANY
claims.note: As claim 12; the card follows the spoken 'on average, about half'.

claims.claim: So the small cells win on numbers, the big cells win on size, and the two cancel out.
claims.note: 'A slope near -1 implies a roughly inverse relation between cell size and count, such that an increase in size by a given factor is offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor'. With slope -0.97 the residual trend in class weight is m^0.03, under 2x across all 26 classes.

claims.claim: THEY CANCEL OUT
claims.note: As claim 14 ('offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor').

claims.claim: Every class ends up holding roughly the same weight.
claims.note: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class'. Heard together with the very next sentence ('With one exception: a dip'), which qualifies 'every' at once, as the paper does ('With the exception of this gap...').

claims.claim: With one exception: a dip, between the fat cells and the muscle fibres.
claims.note: 'prominent biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10^-6 g) and myocytes (near 10^-4 g), separated by a gap of relatively low biomass'; 'With the exception of this gap, all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude'. The paper names the gap as its one exception, so 'one exception' matches. Fig. 4B male: classes near 1e-5 g hold ~0.2-0.3 kg against ~1 kg typical.

claims.claim: ONE DIP
claims.note: As claim 17.

claims.claim: In a typical woman the dip is smaller, and in a typical ten-year-old it is fainter still.
claims.note: 'This gap is also evident but less prominent in the reference female, and is even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child (Fig. 4B)'. Fig. 4B agrees (male muscle peak ~7 kg, female ~4.5 kg, child ~3 kg). 'Typical' renders the paper's 'representative'/'reference' 60-kg female and 32-kg 10-year-old.

claims.claim: TYPICAL WOMAN
claims.note: The paper's representative / reference female (60 kg).

claims.claim: Card 'THE DIP BETWEEN FAT AND MUSCLE': 'TYPICAL MAN: MOST PROMINENT', 'TYPICAL WOMAN: SMALLER', 'TYPICAL 10-YEAR-OLD: FAINTER STILL'
claims.note: Same ranking as the paper: present in the male, 'less prominent in the reference female', 'even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child'; Fig. 4B shows the same order. Text only, so no magnitudes are implied.

claims.claim: Take a typical man.
claims.note: The paper's 'representative male (70 kg)', the ICRP reference male (20-50 y, 176 cm). 'Typical' = 'representative'.

claims.claim: A TYPICAL MAN, sub '70 KG (154 LB)'
claims.note: Reference male 70 kg (abstract, Methods). 70 kg x 2.20462 = 154.3 lb, so 154 lb.

claims.claim: His muscle fibres are fewer than one in fifty thousand of his cells with a nucleus.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: skeletal myocytes 'make up <0.002% of the nucleated cell count' (reference male, ~7 trillion nucleated cells). 0.002% = 1/50,000, and '<' becomes 'fewer than'. 'Muscle fibres' = skeletal myocytes.

claims.claim: Dot grid 250 × 200, caption '50,000 CELLS WITH A NUCLEUS · AT MOST 1 MUSCLE FIBRE', one dot ringed
claims.note: 250 x 200 = 50,000 dots. With <0.002%, at most one fibre per 50,000 nucleated cells, so ringing one dot with 'AT MOST 1' is consistent. (The script's SOURCES entry 11 still calls the caption 'FEWER THAN 1 MUSCLE FIBRE' while entry 18 says 'AT MOST 1'. That is a bookkeeping mismatch in the SOURCES block, not a factual one.)

claims.claim: Yet they make up about half the weight of all his cells.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: 'Cell biomass is dominated by skeletal myocytes, comprising about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass'. SI: skeletal muscle 28 kg minus ~6 kg extracellular minus 0.5 kg stromal leaves 'slightly less than 22 kg of myocyte mass', i.e. ~49% of ~44.3 kg.

claims.claim: ABOUT HALF
claims.note: As claim 27.

claims.claim: And all his cells together weigh about forty-five kilograms.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: '45 kg of cell biomass'; SI: 'a total of ~44.3 kg of cell mass'. 'About forty-five' holds.

claims.claim: 45 KG, sub '99 LB'
claims.note: 45 kg x 2.20462 = 99.2 lb, so 99 lb. (44.3 kg = 97.7 lb, still within the spoken 'about'.)

claims.claim: The other twenty-five of his seventy are not cells at all. They are the water, protein and minerals between them.
claims.note: Fig. 2 caption: cell biomass 'excludes noncellular components of biomass in each tissue, made up of extracellular water, protein, and minerals (~25 kg)'. SI: 'The remaining mass in the 70 kg male resides in extracellular content, including water (18-19 kg), protein (~3.7 kg), and minerals (~3.3 kg, most of which are bone minerals)', together ~25-26 kg. 45 + 25 = 70. 'Between them' renders 'extracellular'.

claims.claim: NOT CELLS, sub '25 KG (55 LB)'
claims.note: ~25 kg extracellular mass; 25 x 2.20462 = 55.1 lb, so 55 lb.

claims.claim: BETWEEN THE CELLS
claims.note: 'Extracellular water, protein, and minerals'.

claims.claim: Bar 'ALL HIS CELLS · 45 KG', half filled 'MUSCLE FIBRES ≈ HALF'; extended by 'NOT CELLS · 25 KG' to '70 KG MAN', 'WATER · PROTEIN · MINERALS'; lengths 45:25
claims.note: 45 kg cells + ~25 kg extracellular = 70 kg reference male; myocytes ~22 of ~44.3 kg ≈ half (SI); the extracellular parts are water, protein and minerals (Fig. 2 caption, SI). The 45:25 proportion matches the figures.

claims.claim: Sort the life in the ocean by size, as it was before industrial fishing, and most size classes held about the same weight too.
claims.note: Abstract: 'biomass within most order of magnitude size classes is indeed remarkably constant, near 1 gigatonne (Gt) wet weight (10^15 g), but bacteria and large marine mammals are markedly above and below this value'. The spectrum is reconstructed for the 'pristine' state 'before industrial-scale human capture of fish and marine mammals (pre-1850)'; today 'the upper one-third of the biomass spectrum has been severely truncated', so the past tense and 'before industrial fishing' are both needed and both present. 'Most' carries the exceptions. Its classes are tenfold, not twofold; the line does not claim otherwise.

claims.claim: THE OCEAN TOO
claims.note: As claim 35.

claims.claim: Ocean card: axis 'SIZE OF SEA LIFE, BACTERIA TO WHALES · LOG SCALE'; level bars titled 'BEFORE INDUSTRIAL FISHING · SCHEMATIC'; first three bars higher, last two lower
claims.note: Fig. 2A (upper 200 m, pristine): the three smallest classes (bacteria + autotrophs) stand at ~2.5, ~2.5 and ~1.9 Gt, the middle classes near ~1 Gt, and the two largest (mammal) classes drop to ~0.1 and ~0.06 Gt. So: first three higher, last two lower, the rest roughly level. Log size axis, 'bacteria to whales' is the paper's title, and 'schematic' is on screen.

claims.claim: And in your body, nobody knows why. No accepted process explains it yet.
claims.note: Discussion: 'To our knowledge, there is no universally recognized process that accounts for these patterns'; Conclusion: 'the developmental mechanisms underlying this pattern remain unresolved'. The paper floats candidate mechanisms (random growth, mismatched growth and division rates) without endorsing any, so 'no accepted process... yet' is the narrow and correct reading. A literature search (Firecrawl research index, 2023-2026) found no later work claiming to explain the human pattern. That search can only fail to break the claim; it confirms nothing under A2, and the cited source dates from 2023.

claims.claim: NOBODY KNOWS WHY / NOT YET EXPLAINED
claims.note: As claim 38. 'Nobody knows why' is a plain rendering of 'no universally recognized process' and 'remain unresolved'.

claims.claim: Trillions of tiny cells, far fewer giant ones, and roughly the same weight at every size.
claims.note: 'Trillions of tiny cells' (≈36 trillion cells, ≈29 trillion of them non-nucleated red cells and platelets) and 'far fewer giant ones' are right. 'At every size' is not. The script itself said four lines earlier that there is one exception, and the paper says the same: 'With the exception of this gap...'. Fig. 4B male: the classes near 1e-5 g hold ~0.2-0.3 kg against ~1 kg elsewhere and ~7 kg at the muscle peak. The closing line takes the exception back. Change: 'at almost every size' (or 'at nearly every size').

claims.claim: ROUGHLY THE SAME (opening and closing card)
claims.note: The paper's 'roughly similar fraction... in each logarithmic cell-size class'. The card carries no 'every'.

claims.claim: Chart axis 'CELL MASS IN GRAMS · LOG SCALE', 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻² g; marks 'RED BLOOD CELLS / FROM 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g', 'FAT CELLS / ~10⁻⁶ g', 'MUSCLE FIBRES / ~10⁻⁴ g'
claims.note: Binning starts 'at red blood cells (4 x 10^-11 g)', the erythrocyte lower bound, hence 'FROM'. The peaks sit at 'adipocytes (near 10^-6 g) and myocytes (near 10^-4 g)'. Fig. 3 data span ~4e-11 to ~3e-3 g, inside the drawn axis. Units and log scale are stated.

claims.claim: 26 size classes, each twice the mass of the one before, the first starting at 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g
claims.note: Methods: 'multiplicative factor of 2... beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'; Fig. 3 caption: '26 logarithmic size classes'. 4e-11 x 2^26 = 2.7e-3 g, which matches the end of the Fig. 3 range.

claims.claim: Bars 'NUMBER OF CELLS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC': a falling staircase with the same dip as the weight bars between the fat and muscle marks
claims.note: Fig. 3: binned counts fall from ~1e13 to ~1e5 along slope -0.97. The largest departure is the pair of bins near 1e-5 g, ~10x below the fit, which sits between the fat (~1e-6) and muscle (~1e-4) marks. On a count axis spanning eight decades, the smaller bumps above the line (~3-5x at the fat and muscle classes) barely register, so a falling staircase with that dip is a fair schematic. It is labelled 'schematic'.

claims.claim: Bars 'WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC': roughly level, with a dip between the fat and muscle marks
claims.note: A6: the drawn shape leaves out half of what the paper reports in this region. The paper describes 'prominent biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10^-6 g) and myocytes (near 10^-4 g), separated by a gap'. In Fig. 4 the peaks rise about as far above the typical class as the dip falls below it. Male (Fig. 4B): muscle classes ~6-7 kg and fat ~3.7 kg against ~1 kg typical, dip ~0.2-0.3 kg. Female on a log axis (Fig. 4A): peaks ~3-5x up, dip ~3-7x down. Bars level at the fat and muscle marks also clash with the spoken claim that muscle fibres hold about half of all cell weight: they occupy only a few of the 26 classes. Change: draw the fat and muscle classes as raised bumps either side of the dip, matching Fig. 4 qualitatively, or drop the weight bars. If the count staircase is redrawn to match, give it the same small bumps.

claims.claim: ABOUT THE SAME
claims.note: Echoes claim 16 ('roughly similar fraction... in each logarithmic cell-size class'). It is shown beside the line that is qualified by the next sentence's dip, and it adds no figure.
